results_lede:
Arm A beats bicubic on structure, consistently but modestly. On far-holdout tiles (Buenos Aires, Melbourne, Johannesburg; 125 tiles), detail correlation rises from 0.273 to 0.333 and SSIM from 0.487 to 0.505. The CNN wins on detail correlation and SSIM in every far tile. Missed-edge chamfer (truth edges to the nearest predicted edge) drops from 12.1 m to 10.1 m, and the CNN wins on 93% of tiles. MAE does not move (1.76 dB), and invented-edge chamfer stays the same (11.3 vs 11.5 m). Near-holdout tiles (Abu Dhabi desert and north Taiwan; 102 tiles) are flatter and harder: detail correlation goes from 0.141 to 0.153 and SSIM from 0.350 to 0.369.

The detail correlation is much higher than Experiment 1’s roughly 0.05, but the tasks differ. NISAR uses the same sensor and acquisition with a 2× grid factor; bicubic already reaches 0.27. The learned model reaches about 0.33.
results_more:
What the extra metrics show

The input-consistency loss is too strict for this data. The real 10 m image, averaged back to 20 m, sits 1.0 dB from the 20 MHz input, because the two products use different parts of the spectrum and carry different speckle. Arm A matches its input to 0.02 dB, far tighter than the truth does. The cost shows in the grid ratio: arm A's pixel steps across input-pixel boundaries are 3.1 times its steps inside them on far tiles, and 6.0 times on near tiles. The truth scores 1.0 and bicubic 1.4. The model imprints the 20 m input grid.

The ablation without consistency (same network, 5,000 steps) trades the other way. MAE falls to 1.68 dB on far tiles and beats bicubic on every tile. The grid ratio falls to 2.0 and invented-edge chamfer to 8.5 m. Detail correlation holds at 0.335. But SSIM drops to 0.462, below bicubic, and missed-edge chamfer rises to 13.4 m. Neither weight is right. Round 2 below tests settings that set the consistency weight so that the model's consistency error lands near the truth's 1 dB floor, or apply the loss to block means at 40 m rather than 20 m.

Scale factor. The x4 arm (5 MHz band B at 80 m to 20 MHz at 20 m, also simultaneous) helps less: detail correlation goes from 0.265 to 0.278 on far tiles and from 0.087 to 0.115 on near tiles. MAE improves on 82% of far tiles, and missed-edge chamfer drops from 64 m to 48 m. Band B is the weak link (QA above). Even with perfect pairing, a 4x jump recovers little detail, in line with Experiment 1's lesson that factor size matters on its own.

Sharpness. All models stay much smoother than the truth (fine-detail energy ratio 0.16 to 0.45). L1 training against a target with about 5 looks of speckle predicts the conditional median, not the speckle. The detail metrics therefore measure structure that L1 can recover, against a target that is itself noisy.
xband_text:
We scored 68 X-band collects over built-up ground: 55 Umbra, 7 ICEYE and 6 Capella (HH, geometry only). Registration converged with a median shift of 11 to 20 m and 40 m correlation of 0.50 to 0.65. We dropped 44 collects with under 10% built-up land, 6 below the 0.2 correlation bar and 2 outside the NISAR swath. Open X-band over the held-out frames is thin, so we also scored collects inside training frames but at least 3 km from every training tile ("train_frame_unseen"). All 6 usable Capella collects fall in that group; the far frames (Buenos Aires and the Philippines) yielded only low-correlation or non-urban Capella scenes.

The CNN reduces the distance from X-band edges to predicted edges. Umbra distances fall from 25.9 m with bicubic to 23.7 m with the CNN; the real 40 MHz image scores 22.7 m. Corresponding values are 34.0, 31.8 and 29.0 m for Capella, and 32.0, 30.4 and 28.7 m for ICEYE. Distances in the reverse direction remain similar. The comparison supports improved edge recall at this scale, while differences in band and viewing geometry limit stronger claims.
transfer_text: The wider windows show modest sharpening of roads, shorelines and field edges beyond bicubic, alongside smooth fields and a faint input-grid pattern. Street grids and building texture in the 40 MHz reference remain unresolved. Native 20 MHz acquisitions show similar behavior, but have no matching higher-bandwidth reference here; those comparisons are visual checks only.
caveats:
• Mixed-mode, not native, 20 MHz in training. The model trained on 20 MHz products cut from 40 MHz echoes. Native 20+5 MHz acquisitions use a different centre frequency and pulse, and possibly a different noise floor. Transfer to them is visual only (no truth exists there).
  • Shared echoes. Input and target share half their spectrum, so their speckle is partly correlated. That holds for any simultaneous pair and matches the deployment question: what would a 40 MHz radar have seen at that moment? It also makes this an easier problem than two separate acquisitions would be.
  • PROVISIONAL data. NISAR L-band products are calibrated but only partly validated. JPL will reprocess them, with validated versions due by the end of 2026. Band B differed by a few tenths of a dB between the two files of one datatake.
  • Round 1 sample. 720 training tiles from 18 frames, 227 held-out tiles from 5 frames, one training seed, no tuning. The consistency weight was not tuned; the ablation shows it matters.
  • Speckled target. The 10 m GCOV has about 5 looks. Detail metrics against it are capped well below 1, and L1 cannot reproduce speckle. Rounds 2 and 3 test multi-date references.
  • X-band sample. Only 13 ICEYE and Capella collects passed, and Capella appears only on unseen ground inside training frames. The X-band check is evidence on edge placement, not a calibrated accuracy.
  • L-band is not C-band. None of this sharpens Sentinel-1. It shows the method works when pairing is clean.
status:
round 1 done Survey; 947 paired tiles from remote HDF5 reads; arm A (x2) and the x4 scale arm on near and far holdouts; consistency ablation; X-band geometry check (Umbra, ICEYE, Capella); transfer panels.

round 2 done Consistency sweep chosen on validation (weight 0.5 at 40 m), now beating bicubic on all five far-holdout metrics; multi-date 40 MHz target (more accurate, smoother); 10 m GCOV to 5 m GSLC (same pattern one level finer); arm B with the X-band edge loss (no gain over arm A′, so X-band stays a validation reference).

rounds 3 and 4 done Additional GSLC dates, gradient loss, longer runs and GAN fine-tuning are reported above. The gradient term gave a small accuracy gain; the GAN increased texture while reducing detail correlation.
